acc57934-ae32-5e43-8f31-305447337577.description2: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.

ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.name: *Suq al-Hamidiyya, Damascus*

ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.second_name: Covered market constructed in the shape of an arcade turning it to the worldwide longest arcade of the fin de siecle
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.description2: The Suq al-Hamidiyya, built in 1886 and 1894, is by far the biggest and most famous suq in Damascus. This bazaar street also links the two most important historic buildings, the Umayyad Mosque and the Citadel. It was built along its western section by incorporating earlier structures, whereas the eastern part of the street was a completely new construction cutting through the existing buildings. The commercial thoroughfare is 450 metres long and 8.70 to 9.90 metres wide, its enormous size and the high standard of its execution accentuate new design principles. So in various respects, this suq is a very interesting example of structural change in a traditional commercial centre.

aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.keywords: Egyptomania; Gaetano Rosellini; university; collector; photograph; anthropology; palaeoethnology; material culture; Florence; Pisa; Egyptology; Nubia; languages; hieroglyph; William Matthew Flinders Petrie; Jacques de Morgan; David Randall-MacIver
aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.description2: The stone grinder was used to pulverise colours or cosmetics. It represents an important relic for the history of the foundation of the Pigorini Museum. Its label, signed by Giglioli, attests that the object was discovered in Thebes by Ernesto Schiaparelli in January 1892 and then donated by him to Giglioli three months later. The grinder cannot be dated as its origins are unknown. As a result of the excavations by W. Petrie and J. De Morgan, who documented the existence of an era preceding the First dynasty, Luigi Pigorini decided to enlarge the Egyptian archaeological collection in the "Museo Preistorico Etnografico e Kircheriano" which he directed at the time. In 1878 he began to acquire important groups, but the main body of the collection was donated by David Randall-MacIver in 1901, from the excavations he carried out on the behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund in the town of el-Amrah, Upper Egypt. In 1905 Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin, offered for purchase the excavation of Hammamiye by the Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt. The last main acquisition took place in 1913 when the Egyptian objects from Enrico Hillyer Giglioli’s collection entered the museum collection.

b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.name: Steam engine building
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.holder: Prussian Palaces (Stiftung Preussische Schlösser und Gärten Berlin Brandenburg)
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.history:
In October 1842 the steam engine in the "Mosque," which could reach 81.4 horsepower, was inaugurated, allowing jets of water from the great fountain in front of Sanssouci Palace to rise to an impressive 38 meters. By possessing what was the most powerful machine in Prussia at the time, built by the young entrepreneur August Borsig, King Frederick William IV hoped to compete with the technical supremacy of England.  
Although today's supply of water to the fountains in Sanssouci Park is provided by means of modern electrical pumps, a visit to the "Mosque" allows the visitor to experience a technical marvel from days past that is still in operation.
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.keywords: Moorish style; Romanticism; Sanssouci; Potsdam; exoticism; steam engine; steam pumping; Frederick William IV; gardens
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.description2: The Steam Engine Building, located on a bay of the Havel River called the Neustädter Havelbucht, is at once the most charming as well as the most exotic building in Potsdam. Frederick William IV, the "Romantic on the throne," had it built by Ludwig Persius from 1841-1843, "in the style of the Turkish mosques, with a minaret as a smokestack." The building, which could still be seen at that time from Sanssouci Palace, added a picturesque architectural accent to the Potsdam cultural landscape.

b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.name: Haydarpaşa Train Station
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Train Station
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.description2: In 1871 Sultan Abdülaziz ordered a rail line to be built from Haydarpaşa to İzmit. Haydarpaşa station opened in 1872, and in 1888 the Anatolian Railway (CFOA) took over the line and the station. Since the station was built next to the Bosporus, freight trains would unload at Haydarpaşa and the freight would be transferred to ships. Haydarpaşa was chosen to be the northern terminus of the Baghdad Railway and the Hijaz Railway in 1904 and with rail traffic increasing, a new and larger building was required. The Anatolian Railway hired two German architects; Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu to build the new building. They chose a neo-classical structure and construction started in 1906.

b29cbfc5-92ab-5924-883e-7d561e5c7761.description2: This drawing of the temples and fountains of Zaghwan was drawn by Sir Grenville Temple in the mid-19th century. The triumphal arc and the nymphaeum are carved with two important tales from the city's ancient history. This water temple, located at the feet of Mount Zaghwan, contains a 30 metre long semicircle nymphaeum, bordered on the inside by arched galleries fitted with various niches. At its feet lies a pool, flowing with water which is then carried all the way to Carthage.

b33144e1-5551-5a5c-a7ba-4cefefd46e94.name: Funeral statue of Lady Khent and her youngest child
b33144e1-5551-5a5c-a7ba-4cefefd46e94.description: The funerary statues of the *mastaba* tombs in the Old Kingdom were kept in sealed rooms called *serdabs*. The statues were believed to be alter egos of the deceased, apt to receive the mortuary rites, which were then completed in the adjacent tomb chapel. Khen (full name, Khentit-ka) was the wife of a high official. The sculpture is a magnificent example of the Old Kingdom canonical sculpture in the round.

b34a6459-d73e-575a-bf25-d6eeecca51a1.name: *The Opening of the Suez Canal*
b34a6459-d73e-575a-bf25-d6eeecca51a1.author: Marina Minozzi
b34a6459-d73e-575a-bf25-d6eeecca51a1.keywords: Sculptors; route; travel; waterway; Austria; Lloyd; Assicurazioni Generali; Bourse; Adriatic; Egypt; Said; Ismail; Pasha; Ferdinand de Lesseps; Suez Canal Company; Compagnie universelle du canal maritime de Suez; vice-president; Cairo; India
b34a6459-d73e-575a-bf25-d6eeecca51a1.description2: The artist Pietro Magni studied at the Academy of Brera, travelled to Rome in 1849 and battled for the Roman Republic. His first artwork as mentioned in the author’s biography is *The First Steps*, known though the photographs to have been on display at the International Exhibition in London in 1862. In 1863 the businessman Pietro Revoltella commissioned the artist to create a marble group showing the opening of the Suez Canal, now in the Revoltella Museum in Trieste. It shows how important the project was for the commissioner, confident that the new opening toward the East would offer economic advantages to his city. Unfortunately he died two months before seeing the Suez Canal completed. The sculpture shows a classical allegory with Europe uniting the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea, behind them the genius of commerce with winged feet indicating the canal the unifies Europe and Asia.

b623eb8c-a4d4-585a-b9d5-23a452054f55.name: *Egypt, San. View of the excavations.*
b623eb8c-a4d4-585a-b9d5-23a452054f55.second_name: Taken from the photo album of Emmanuel de Rougé's mission to Egypt, where he was accompanied by Viscount Aymard de Banville and Jacques de Rougé
b623eb8c-a4d4-585a-b9d5-23a452054f55.description2: Emmanuel de Rougé was a French egyptologist who continued the work of Champollion. He was a member of l'Academie des Sciences, the curator of the "Musée Égyptien" of the Musée du Louvre (1849), professor of Egyptian archaeology at the Collège de France (1864), and authored many works on the history of Egypt. In 1862, he was sent on a mission to Egypt where he travelled along the Nile from the Delta to the cataracts, on a boat which had been loaned to the mission by Isma'il Pasha. This mission was the subject of a report and an illustrated publication with photographs by the Viscount Aymard de Banville. This photograph was taken at San, also known as the ancient site of Tanis, where the archaeologist Mariette was directing an excavation.

b776a817-c7d7-51b1-8767-4441833fd7a5.name: *The Progress of Steam: A View in White Chapel Road, 1830*

b776a817-c7d7-51b1-8767-4441833fd7a5.description2: Steam engines carried a great variety of goods in the 1830s. This English cartoon imagines the chaos the widespread use of collective and individual carbon-fuelled transport systems would bring (pollution, noise, cumbersome, etc.) to one of London's great arteries, Whitechapel Road. These vehicles provided fashionable services such as on-board coffee.

b7a9c747-adba-50e0-a0a8-312875639e02.name: Gold bracelet
b7a9c747-adba-50e0-a0a8-312875639e02.description2: Based closely on Assyrian reliefs. Illustrates Assyrian influence on 19th century jewellery.

b7e5dd09-cf9b-5310-9343-8db43d0c9114.name: *The Emperor of Austria ascending the Great Pyramid*
b7e5dd09-cf9b-5310-9343-8db43d0c9114.description2: William Simpson wrote in his autobiography: "I went out one day and saw the Emperor of Austria lugged to the top of the Great Pyramid by two Arabs as if he had been only an overland passenger". Many visitors were unceremoniously hauled to the top of the monument by local inhabitants, helping unfit and often overweight tourists to clamber up the huge blocks. Emperor Franz Joseph was one of many European dignitaries in Egypt in November 1869 for the opening of the Suez Canal. Simpson was employed by the Illustrated London News as their "Special Artist". Photography would soon replace such drawings.

b8bb387e-75d0-55d8-89ae-9322c204928c.name: Simplon-Orient Express Poster
b8bb387e-75d0-55d8-89ae-9322c204928c.description2: The Orient Express, owned by the Wagon-Lits Company, connected Paris and Istanbul between 1883 and 1977. French, German, Austrian and Ottoman diplomats and civil servants were on board for its first journey. In the early years, the travellers stayed in different hotels in Istanbul but starting from 1895, passengers stayed exclusively in Pera Palace, which was bought by the Wagon-Lits Company. The Orient Express did not run during World War I, from 1914 to 1918.

b8f1e03b-6dae-584b-990b-f69d7ae90efe.name: Beacon to a new world
b8f1e03b-6dae-584b-990b-f69d7ae90efe.description2: Flinders Petrie purchased this figurine in Giza. He was informed by the seller that it had been unearthed at a site in the western Nile Delta. Petrie recognised the Cypriot and Egyptian influences and headed to the region where the figurine was said to have been found. It is here that he found Naukratis.

ba3b8c6f-86e6-5a4a-9b9a-6d600f5e1009.name: Archaeological excavations
ba3b8c6f-86e6-5a4a-9b9a-6d600f5e1009.description2: Portrait of three scholars in front of the tent camp during the excavations in the archaeological area of Saqqara, Giza in 1912. The paper photograph was printed from a gelatine print negative.

bc794754-d095-53e4-90c2-e4f2b5406077.name: Assyrianising pendant
bc794754-d095-53e4-90c2-e4f2b5406077.description2: Gold pendant made in Rome based on an Assyrian winged bull, now famous throughout Europe. Illustrates Assyrian influence on 19th-century jewellery.

bd196d3c-3ad7-5a3c-a7bf-f9e67e2fa612.name: *The Library of Hadrian*
bd196d3c-3ad7-5a3c-a7bf-f9e67e2fa612.author: Tsigkakou 1981, 200-201
bd196d3c-3ad7-5a3c-a7bf-f9e67e2fa612.artist: Théodore Achille Louis, Vicomte du Moncel
bd196d3c-3ad7-5a3c-a7bf-f9e67e2fa612.description2: This representation is entitled *Painted Stoa*, referring to the colonnade (stoa) with monumental columns depicted on the right side of the picture. Nineteenth-century visitors to Athens referred to this monument by various names, such as Painted Stoa of Hadrian or Gymnasium, for its true identity was not discovered until after 1884, when systematic excavations commenced in the area of the Roman Agora (Forum Romanum). Recent archaeological investigation shows that this imposing colonnade is part of the propylon of the Library of Hadrian. Depicted at the edge of the propylon-incorporated in two columns- is a small Byzantine church. This is Hagioi Asomatoi sta Skalia (Incorporeal Saints at the Steps) of the eleventh century, and was demolished before the end of the nineteenth century, falling victim to the antiquarian extremism of ‘purifying archaeological sites’. The works of the artist-travellers who flooded into Greece during the nineteenth century are tangible testimonies not only to the illustrious past, but also to the landscape.

en: Tsigakou, Fani-Maria, *The Rediscovery of Greece: Travellers and Painters of the Romantic Era*, London: Thames & Hudson, 1981.

be44b9c0-4045-581b-a6e2-85c0f3bcd137.name: The Austrian ship on which Emperor Franz Joseph participated at the opening ceremony of the Suez Canal in 1869
be44b9c0-4045-581b-a6e2-85c0f3bcd137.holder: Austrian Military Museum / Institute of Military History
be44b9c0-4045-581b-a6e2-85c0f3bcd137.description2: Emperor Franz Joseph visited the Suez Canal on board the Austrian ship, *Elisabeth*. He reached the Egyptian port of Ismilia on 14 Nov 1869 and stayed in Egypt until the 26 Nov 1869. During this trip, he also visited Cairo and Alexandria.

bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.name: *Works for the opening of the Corinth Canal*
bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.author: Maria Dimitriadou
bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.description2:
The Corinth Canal under constuction, circa 1885. Photographer unknown.  
The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnesian peninsula from the Greek. The idea of the canal was revived after Greece gained independence but soon abandoned due to economical reasons. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave an new impetus and the following year, the Zaimis government passed a law authorising the construction of the canal, which was formally inaugurated on 23 April 1882. Zaimis assigned the project to the Hungarian István Türr who set up the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe but the company failed and the project was finished by the company of Andeas Syngros. The canal was designed by the Hungarian engineer Béla Gerster with the assistance of the French Vincent Dauzants, a chief engineer of the Suez canal.

c183f4c0-12ee-5c65-bc23-c8e71cccb311.name: Qusayr Amra
c183f4c0-12ee-5c65-bc23-c8e71cccb311.dates: AD 8th century; visited by Alois Musil in 1896
c183f4c0-12ee-5c65-bc23-c8e71cccb311.author: Mohammad Najjar
c183f4c0-12ee-5c65-bc23-c8e71cccb311.history: The best-known of the desert castles and a World Heritage Site. This monument was most probably built sometime between 723 and 743, by al-Walid Ibn Yazid, the future Umayyad caliph Walid II. The abandoned structure was re-discovered by Alois Musil in 1898, with the frescoes made famous in drawings by an Austrian artist named Mielich for Musil's book.
c183f4c0-12ee-5c65-bc23-c8e71cccb311.keywords: World Heritage Site; Alois Musil; rediscovery; archaeological investigation
c183f4c0-12ee-5c65-bc23-c8e71cccb311.description2: Qusayr Amra is one of few Jordanian sites that have been listed as a World Heritage site. It represents the formative stage of Islamic art and architecture. It consists of vaulted reception hall and a bath house the walls of which were richly decorated. Its famous figurative wall paintings are proof that figurative art was not prohibited outside religious contexts at least during the first two centuries of Islam.

c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.name: Tripolitania (Libya). Italian soldiers in front of a Roman mosaic
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.holder: Central Institute for Cataloguing and Documentation (ICCD)
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.author: Giulia Barrera
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.description2:
Italian soldiers in front of a Roman mosaic in Tripolitania, Libya. At their feet, almost at the centre of the photo, a plaque explains that: “These wonderful remains of Ancient Rome art and civilization” have been brought back to the admiration of posterity by the Italian soldiers of the Bersaglieri 33rd Battalion in 1911 and they “confirm… Italy’s right to rule over Tripolitania”.  
The plaque explicitly claims that Italy colonial ambitions over Libya were legitimate because Ancient Rome had once ruled over that territory. This line of argument was often used by Italian colonialists in order to legitimize Italian colonial ambitions over Libya.

ca4bf20e-94a9-50b1-bca9-38b4f7855c35.keywords: archaeology; exploration; Egyptomania; travel; traveller; collection; collector; museums; historical document
ca4bf20e-94a9-50b1-bca9-38b4f7855c35.description2: A watercolour scene showing the king before various gods from the tomb of Seti I in the Valley of the Kings, Thebes, drawn by Henry Salt shortly after the discovery of the tomb by the explorer Giovanni Belzoni in 1817. The freshness of the colours amazed the early travellers.

cb52291b-7b0d-5472-b972-2e4f32848e2f.description2: Early stereoview of the Assyrian Court at the Crystal Palace. Based on recent discoveries by Layard, who wrote the guidebook.

cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.name: *Bisotun, geometric drawing of a bas-relief*
cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.artist: Engraver: A. Guillaumet; artist: Pascal-Xavier Coste; author: Eugène Flandin
cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.second_name: Taken from Eugène Flandin and Pascal Coste's *Voyage en Perse*, which took place from 1840 to 1841.
cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.description2: In 1840, the painter Eugène Flandin (1809–1876) and the architect and painter Pascal Coste (1787–1879) were sent on mission to Persia by l'Institut de France in order to write up an inventory of the country's past and contemporary riches, and to renew the political and economic ties between France and Persia. The mission was directed by Édouard de Sercey, who soon returned to France. However, despite the trying conditions, Flandin and Coste were able to stay for two more years and collected an impressive archive documenting the sites they explored. This is a print of one of the bas-reliefs in Mount Behistun (Iran), which  Darius had carved during the 6th century BC.

cbf85605-4ba0-5a95-83bb-a01c29a67fc3.name: The Rosetta Stone
cbf85605-4ba0-5a95-83bb-a01c29a67fc3.keywords: archaeology; Egyptomania; exploration; collection; collecting; inscription; museums; travel; traveller; historical document
cbf85605-4ba0-5a95-83bb-a01c29a67fc3.description2: A letter from General Lord Hely Hutchinson, Commander of the British army in Alexandria, Egypt, to the traveller and scientist Edward Daniel Clarke. Clarke is to ensure the security of the Rosetta Stone which he, W.R. Hamilton and Colonel Turner are acquiring from the French army under the terms of the Capitulation of Alexandria. The letter also asks Clarke to copy the inscription from the Stone. It is dated September 13, 1801.

cc27cb2b-74b2-53c7-99e4-842dcfe24334.name: The post office
cc27cb2b-74b2-53c7-99e4-842dcfe24334.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
cc27cb2b-74b2-53c7-99e4-842dcfe24334.history: Following the establishment of the French Protectorate in Tunisia, the French administration set up the post and telegraphy service in the Regency of Tunis. The post and telegraph office was created on 1 July 1888. The first Tunisian stamp was issued the following day. Finally, the Hôtel des Postes de Tunis was opened on the 11 July 1882. The first telegraph lines connecting Tunis and Marseille were soon built, and the first international communication was effectuated in November 1915 between Tunisia and Algeria.
cc27cb2b-74b2-53c7-99e4-842dcfe24334.description2: The Hôtel des PTT was designed by the architect Henri Saladin, and built on the Rue d'Italie (now called Rue Charles-de-Gaulle) in a network of straight roads lined with apartment blocks. This imposing building is designed in a Greco-Roman style. The windowless arches and huge wall clock on the main façade hint to the enormous dimensions of this municipal building's great hall. It was listed as a historic monument in 1992.

ccc527b3-f647-5b4d-83e5-d6c24cd38f9e.name: Archaeological excavations
ccc527b3-f647-5b4d-83e5-d6c24cd38f9e.description2: This photograph shows the entrance to a tomb made of granite, discovered in the archaeological area of Saqqara. At the entrance of the tomb appears the renowned archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt accompanied by his wife. The photograph dates to 1904.

cd05b644-c357-52ab-89b2-eb3a5e54560e.description2: Figurines based on the Assyrian sculptures were popular collecting pieces. Owners displayed their interest current events. Buyers included the rich and famous, as well as museums. These Parian ware figurines were also exhibited. Winged bull.

cd191826-9521-5bf9-9d19-dd2913e5662a.name: Egyptian vases
cd191826-9521-5bf9-9d19-dd2913e5662a.dates: 3800–3500 BC; bought by Mihail C. Sutu in 1870
cd191826-9521-5bf9-9d19-dd2913e5662a.description2: In 1870 historian, numismatist and academician Mihail C. Șutu travelled to Egypt accompanied by his wife. They took a cruise on the Nile, visited Cairo, where he studied antique Egyptian units of measure for weight (one of his of domains of interest). A passionate collector, he purchased a series of Egyptian coins and antiquities, among which some vessels that are considered to be part of a funerary inventory and have been dated in the first phase of the Naqada culture (c. 3900–3300 BC).

d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.name: Al-Madina al-Munawwara Station
d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.holder: Saudi Commission for Tourism and Antiquities
d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.history:
The Hijaz railway was very important for the Islamic world where pilgrims could reach al-Hijaz safe and in short time comparing to what was before. The station was known in al-Madina as *istasyon*, a Turkish word meaning station.  
The station is located west of the Prophet 's Mohammed (PBU) Mosque and approximately 1 km a way, in the region now known Aanbariyah beside Anbariyah Mosque and Alanbariyah Gate, which was removed for the purpose of expanding the streets in the area.  
The first train arrived to al-Madina in 23rd of August 1908 and the official ceremony for the opening of the Station was held a week later.
d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.keywords: Hijaz; railway station; pilgrimage; hajj; pilgrimage route; caravan; sacred places; communication; innovation; architecture; Arabian Peninsula; Ottoman; Germany; Abdul Hamid; abd al-hamid
d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.architects: Mukhtar bey, the general manager of the line
d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.description2: The station is rectangular in shape with a length of about 700 meters and a width of about 150 meters, and is surrounded by a fence built of black basalt stone, and comprises a set of 11 buildings including the main one. All the station buildings and remaining trains and carriages were restored by the Saudi commission for Tourism and Antiquities and converted into an Islamic museum for the city of al-Madina.

d1281641-f7a2-5961-be72-73fcc5949104.name: Telegraph transmitter
d1281641-f7a2-5961-be72-73fcc5949104.keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication
d1281641-f7a2-5961-be72-73fcc5949104.description2: The primary reasons for the Ottoman Empire adopting the telegram earlier and more easily than railroads were the telegram's convenience and lack of cost. American scientist Lawrence Smith – using tools sent by Samuel Morse – made a successful trial in front of the Sultan Abdulmecid, who was interested in technological innovations and science, and began modernization of the empire. Due to the outbreak of the Crimean War, the first underwater telegraph line was established between Crimea and Istanbul. This telegraph transmitter (1912, Siemens & Halske) was used in Istanbul in World War I.

He depicted real landscapes, people and animals. In 1864 the painter went to Pompei and Paestum where he made a series of studies of archeological ruins discovered in that period from excavation campaigns promoted by the new Italian State.

d3253a8b-e29d-5956-a599-90638d365b17.name: The Flood Tablet
d3253a8b-e29d-5956-a599-90638d365b17.keywords: archaeology; exploration; travel; traveller; collection; museums; cuneiform; inscription; clay; Gilgamesh; science
d3253a8b-e29d-5956-a599-90638d365b17.description2: Inspired by Layard’s discoveries, George Smith began to study cuneiform. His dedication was rewarded with the amazing discovery of a version of the Biblical Flood Story. The British Prime Minister came to his lecture. The news amazed the world. The Daily Telegraph financed an expedition to Nineveh to find the missing piece. Having found it, Smith died of fever on his way home.

d6d5f11a-71c5-5934-871d-7aa7c6836d79.name: Henry Salt’s 1817 excavations at the Pyramids and Sphinx
d6d5f11a-71c5-5934-871d-7aa7c6836d79.keywords: archaeology; exploration; Egyptomania; travel; traveller; collection; collector; museums
d6d5f11a-71c5-5934-871d-7aa7c6836d79.description2: On his arrival in Egypt, Salt sponsored and recorded the excavations of Captain Giovanni Battista Caviglia at the Giza pyramids and Sphinx. Caviglia discovered new chambers in the Great Pyramid and a lost chapel beneath the head of the Sphinx.

d815fe5d-36cb-5efe-b0e0-241a5e5e2941.name: Stamp sketch
d815fe5d-36cb-5efe-b0e0-241a5e5e2941.keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication
d815fe5d-36cb-5efe-b0e0-241a5e5e2941.description2: The Ottoman Empire held a contest to determine the stamp that would be printed in London between 1919 and 1921. Stamp sketches drawn by famous calligraphers are exhibited in the museum. This stamp sketch belonged to the Eminönü Post Office.

d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.name: Water pumping equipment in Kağıthane, Istanbul
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; History of Water in Ottoman Empire; Water Pump Station
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.description2: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.

d8832d40-d884-5998-a0e8-a3f9f85b3dea.name: The Robert Muawad Private Museum
d8832d40-d884-5998-a0e8-a3f9f85b3dea.author: Julien El Khoury, Jeff El-Msanne, Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
d8832d40-d884-5998-a0e8-a3f9f85b3dea.history: The Robert Muawad Private Museum was a private residence in Beirut's Zokak el-Blat neighbourhood that the Lebanese businessman Robert Muawad turned into a museum. It is located in Beirut's central district, and contains a mix of local, Western and orientalist artefacts. The palace itself was built in 1911 near the Grand Serail, and is decorated with wooden panels dating to the 14th to 19th centuries. Muawad acquired this historical state-of-the-art residence to host his precious collection of fine arts and antique pieces.
d8832d40-d884-5998-a0e8-a3f9f85b3dea.keywords: museum; antiques; art; collection; cultures; traditions; heritage; Palace; Museum; Robert Muawad; Beirut
d8832d40-d884-5998-a0e8-a3f9f85b3dea.description2: The collection, housed in the luxurious Pharaun Palace, contains a vast and rare collection of antiques, books and manuscripts, objets d'art, Byzantine mosaics, Roman marble sculptures, ancient weaponry and treasures such as clocks, carpets, metal work, Chinese and Islamic pottery as well as jewellery and precious stones. The magnificent interior includes original wood panelling dating from the 14th to 19th centuries, and reflects the grand exterior and the palace's setting in expansive and beautiful gardens. The palace was built in the neo-gothic style in 1911 and reflects the Pharaun's infatuation with so-called "Islamic art", especially following his numerous travels to Syria.

d903044a-9099-5fe4-8bcc-00c31c453207.description2: Architectural elevation of the ruins of the Roman aqueducts of Caesaria Maritima in Palestine by C.R. Conder, R.E., dated 6 April, 1873. In addition to the geographical features of the land, the olive groves and other agricultural features and the villages, the SWP recorded all of the visible archaeological remains of the country.

d993a25c-fe0f-55cb-b4fb-77d8dd825454.keywords: Egyptomania; Thebes; Karnak; Memphis; papyrology; epigraphy; Alexandria; Cairo; Ferdinand de Lesseps; Napoleon Bonaparte; Vienna; Berlin; collector; Egyptology; Nubia; languages; diplomacy; Muhammad Ali; Charles X; Louvre; Cailliaud; Henry Salt; botany

d993a25c-fe0f-55cb-b4fb-77d8dd825454.description2: The drawing shows the arrangement of Drovetti's collection inside the right wing of the building of the Academy of Sciences in 1852. The wall decoration mimics a wall of green stone tiles. The organisation of this room remained roughly unchanged until 2006. The institution of the Egyptian Museum in Turin marked an essential stage in the rediscovery of Egypt and followed the interpretation of hieroglyphics by Champollion. In 1824 King Carlo Felice of Savoy bought the collection of Egyptian antiquities gathered together by Bernardino Drovetti, general consul of France in Egypt from 1803 to 1830, in order to give to the Piedmontese capital an archaeological museum able to compete with all the other museums around Europe. The Drovetti’s collection was donated to the University Museum together with other Egyptian monuments already part of Savoy's collection. This collection already included more than five thousand pieces including statues (one of them is the famous statue of Rameses II), steles, offering tables, wood and bronze objects, mummies, furniture, jewellery, other materials and a significant number of papyri. A catalogue of the collection was made by Champollion around the 1820s.

en: Peyrot, A., *Torino nei secoli. Vedute e pliante, feste e cerimonie nell’incisione dal Cinquecento all’Ottocento*, vol. 2, Turin: Tipografia Torinese Editrice, 1965, pl. 542/16: 778.

d9b9133d-3db3-50b8-9527-532bd887cb5c.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
d9b9133d-3db3-50b8-9527-532bd887cb5c.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
d9b9133d-3db3-50b8-9527-532bd887cb5c.description2: This image represents the vignette on the title page of Volume 3 to 'The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt and Nubia' from drawings made on the spot by David Roberts, lithographed by Louis Haghe and published in six volumes by F.G. Moon in London between 1842-1845. It is entitled 'Temple of El Khasne, Petra' and shows the spectacular treasury of Petra as seen by travellers approaching the ancient city through the famous, steep and narrow ravine. Petra had remained forgotten until rediscovered by the Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in 1812. Subsequently, it became one of the romantic fascinations of European Orientalist artists and writers.Roberts visited Petra in early March 1839, and he wrote that it was 'probably one of the greatest challenges on earth to a painter'.

The relief shows the goddess Maat, recognised by the feather on her head.

dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.name: Map of the Red Sea
dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)
dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.archival: *The Red Sea Pilot ... With directions for the navigation of the Suez Canal. Second edition. \[Compiled by J. C. Richards\]*, *Sailing Directions. Red Sea*, London: Hydrographic Office, 1883, third edition
dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.keywords: Trade; route; port; Great Britain; India; coffee; Red Sea; Yemen; Mocha; British settlement on the route to India; communication; telegraph; telegraph between ports; Suez Canal; pilgrimage; Makka; Arab Peninsula; Holy places
dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.description2:
*The Red Sea Pilot* included sailing indications and directions for navigation from the Suez Canal to the strait of Bab el-Mandeb, including Aqaba, Jeddah and the coast of Hijaz as far as Aden.  
  
Trading activity (especially in grain) between the two coasts of the Red Sea and the maritime traffic after the opening of the Suez Canal were fundamental economic activities, hence the importance of reliable knowledge of navigation routes, sailing directions, climate, winds and currents. In addition to the local ships used to carry pilgrims to Mecca and for trading activity, European ships crossed the Red Sea. The book also provides information about the main ports and their facilities. For example, it states that the telegraph had been installed from Suez to Swakin and from Swakin to Jeddah, and that there was telegraph communication between Aden, Suez, Bombay and the Cape of Good Hope.

e1b84d6c-9cc4-503f-aaf7-19adce734645.name: Petra
e1b84d6c-9cc4-503f-aaf7-19adce734645.type: World Heritage Site; archaeological site; Nabatean city
e1b84d6c-9cc4-503f-aaf7-19adce734645.author: Mohammad Najjar
e1b84d6c-9cc4-503f-aaf7-19adce734645.history: Petra's history goes back to prehistoric times, but its most famous monuments are from the Hellenistic and Nabataean periods. After the annexation of the Nabataean state by the Romans in 106 AD, Petra became part of the Roman Province of Arabia. The city continued to be important during the Late Antiquity and Islamic periods. Two fortresses were built in the vicinity of Petra during the Crusader period.
e1b84d6c-9cc4-503f-aaf7-19adce734645.keywords: Heritage; Nabataean; Roman; Late Antiquity; monuments; the Siq; Burckhardt
e1b84d6c-9cc4-503f-aaf7-19adce734645.description2: Petra is the crown jewel of Jordanian heritage. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1986. The most prominent monuments of Petra are the Siq, the Treasury, the Winged Lions Temple, the Great Temple, Qasr al-Bint Temple, the monastery, the theatre, the church with mosaic floors and many other monuments.

e2b48175-dfa4-5317-9f12-0d280735f099.name: Drawing of the railway bridge between the mainland and Venice
e2b48175-dfa4-5317-9f12-0d280735f099.description2: This panoramic view shows the railway link between Venice and the mainland. In 1837 a company was founded to organize the building of the railway in the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. Construction started in 1840 and the railway reached the Venetian station of Santa Lucia in 1846.

e3b28f28-4ce6-5e60-9902-8e13ef295f77.name: Photograph of Tétouan Railway Station
e3b28f28-4ce6-5e60-9902-8e13ef295f77.description: The image does not give one a sense of the real scale of Tétouan Railway Station, one of the first to be built in Morocco in 1918, covering an area of about 1,200m2 and comprises three buildings: one castle-shaped and two large hangars. The station is a model of colonial architecture, bearing the signature of Julio Rodriguez Roda, an engineer working for the Spanish Society of Colonisation, which was responsible for many structures in northern Morocco. Receiving its first travellers at the end of World War I, the line stretched from Tétouan to Ceuta, calling at Martil, Ben Karrich and Zinat.

e3d1028e-c33d-53a4-a895-0276547994a0.name: *Construction of the Bordeaux bridge in 1821*
e3d1028e-c33d-53a4-a895-0276547994a0.second_name: Taken from the collection *Topographie de la France*, "Département de la Gironde"
e3d1028e-c33d-53a4-a895-0276547994a0.description2: The construction of bridges had always been a complicated matter, and particularly so in Bordeaux, where the river was especially temperamental. Until the 19th century people crossed it by ferry. However, in 1810 Napoléon I ordered a bridge to be built in Bordeaux, which was completed in 1822. The expertise this required (particularly the building of tunnels to reduce the size of the structure) attracted the attention of many contemporary engineers and architects.

e5b5e193-f08b-5657-b562-1f2add9c333b.name: *Egyptian Landscape*
e5b5e193-f08b-5657-b562-1f2add9c333b.description: This was a good example for the author to derive information from because the author himself did not travel to the Near East. The painter documented his works thanks to books with prints or photographs. It could be located at the Kom Ombo temple in the east bank of the Nile valley.

e5dcb5be-a7f2-5f24-b1e8-fae35ee4b7b5.name: *Foundations of Haram al-Sharif*
e5dcb5be-a7f2-5f24-b1e8-fae35ee4b7b5.description2: Foundations of the South-Eastern corner of the Haram es-Sharif, as revealed for the first time by Charles Warren. This tunnel was some 85 feet below ground. Warren’s team were experienced mining engineers, and were assisted, as shown in several of this sequence of watercolours by William ‘Crimea’ Simpson, sent to record the expedition for the Illustrated London News, by extremely courageous local Jerusalem residents.

e6ce0745-bf5d-5a64-ab65-c5f97224e8ef.description2: On the occasion of the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored under the direction of the archeologist and topographer Rodolfo Lanciani. The site housed the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to the Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the ex provinces. Every single nation participated through original reproductions of archaeological materials, often lost. The photo shows material evidence and casts coming from Greece.

e77f7585-833b-5120-a08a-4e03b131f833.name: *Interior of the Great Temple at Baalbec*
e77f7585-833b-5120-a08a-4e03b131f833.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
e77f7585-833b-5120-a08a-4e03b131f833.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
e77f7585-833b-5120-a08a-4e03b131f833.artist: Drawn by William Henry Bartlett; engraved by Ebenezar Challis
e77f7585-833b-5120-a08a-4e03b131f833.description2: This view into the interior of the Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek, Lebanon originally formed appeared in 'Syria, The Holy Land, Asia Minor, &c', illustrated views printed in 3 series over 2 volumes (37 plates, 37 plates, and 48 plates for each series respectively) including maps and title pages. The publication resulted from the 1836-1838 collaboration between the painter William Henry Bartlett, the engraver Ebenezer Challis and the Publishers Fisher, Son and Co. The architectural and artistic details they recorded subsequently inspired European Neoclassical architects and artists such as Robert Adam, who based one of the ceilings at Osterley House on the ceiling of the Temple of Bacchus and the portico of St George's, Bloomsbury on its portico. Since the 1860s, many tourists visited the site, including, in 1898, the German emperor Wilhelm II. Struck by the magnificence of the ruins, he dispatched a German archaeological team, whose subsequent work resulted in a meticulous, illustrated publication that further popularised the site.

e89aa553-0859-53ef-ad91-bdaddb8ac231.name: *Hüdavendigar* Paper in Armenian
e89aa553-0859-53ef-ad91-bdaddb8ac231.description2: After the *Tanzimat* (reforms), newspapers in Arabic, Persian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Albanian, Kurdish, English, French, Italian and German began appearing in the Ottoman Empire. Some of them were bilingual as Turkish-Greek, Turkish-Armenian and Turkish-Arabic. *Hüdavendigar* was a provincial newspaper of Bursa and it was first published on 19 February 1869. The same year, starting with the 80th issue, the back page was printed in Armenian. The paper was published twice (Wednesday and Saturday) and then four times a week. It was 50 x 25 cm. Subscription for a year was 100 kuruş, for six months was 50 kuruş and one issue was 20 para (1/2 kuruş). It continued to be published until 1953 under different names.

e8e2873a-17d1-558a-a507-0fd33c1cc8ae.name: Palette
e8e2873a-17d1-558a-a507-0fd33c1cc8ae.holder: National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography “Luigi Pigorini”
e8e2873a-17d1-558a-a507-0fd33c1cc8ae.author: Marina Minozzi
e8e2873a-17d1-558a-a507-0fd33c1cc8ae.keywords: Egyptomania; Gaetano Rosellini; university; collector; photograph; anthropology; palaeoethnology; material culture; Florence; Pisa; Egyptology; Nubia; languages; hieroglyph; William Matthew Flinders Petrie; Jacques de Morgan; David Randall-MacIver
e8e2873a-17d1-558a-a507-0fd33c1cc8ae.description2: The cosmetic palette is fish-shaped and reproduces the form of a fish from the Nile River, *Tilapia nilotica*. The palette was found in a woman's tomb along with a turtle-shaped cosmetic palette, ivory findings, a comb, a huge ring and ceramics. As a result of the excavations by W. Petrie and J. De Morgan, who documented the existence of an era preceding the 1st dynasty, Luigi Pigorini, director of the "Museo Preistorico Etnografico e Kircheriano”, decided to expand the Egyptian archaeological collection. In 1878 he began to acquire important groups, but the main body of the collection was donated by David Randall-MacIver in 1901, after the excavations he carried out on the behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund in the town of el-Amrah, Upper Egypt. Another major purchase — from the Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt (excavations of Hammamiye) led by Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin — followed in 1905. The last main acquisition took place in 1913 when the Egyptian objects from Enrico Hillyer Giglioli’s collection entered the museum collection.

en: Cappozzo, M., “La collezione egizia del Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico ‘Luigi Pigorini’”, in *Bullettino di Paletnologia Italiana*, Roma, Istituto Poligrafico e Zecca dello Stato, (2005–2007), 96: 131–202, cat. 69.

e8fa6bb3-c6a3-5e41-9e45-50c1fbee8ea8.name: *Excavation in Giza*
e8fa6bb3-c6a3-5e41-9e45-50c1fbee8ea8.description: Hermann Junker with Egyptian workers excavating a statue from the mastaba of Schepsesptah in 1913. The German-born Egyptologist Hermann Junker became a professor at the University of Vienna in 1909. In 1911 the Austrian Academy obtained the concession for excavation in Giza. In 1912 Hermann Junker's team started to excavate tombs close to the pyramids of Giza.

e9e0d077-22ec-5da6-8968-784248276025.name: Palais Kasr el-Said
e9e0d077-22ec-5da6-8968-784248276025.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
e9e0d077-22ec-5da6-8968-784248276025.history: Located near the Bardo palaces, this palace had belonged to a noble of the Husainid court until 1867. It was then subject to a series of adjustments and expansions under the reign of Sadok Pacha Bey, who took up residence there once the works were completed. It was in this palace that, on 12 May 1881, Sadok Pacha Bey added his signature to the treaty which would impose a French Protectorate on his country, headed by General Bréart. The building was restored and taken over by l'Institut National du Patrimonie in 1988, and now houses the first landmarks of the Musée d'Histoire de la Tunisie Moderne et Contemporaine, whilst also preserving its Husainid foundations. It also holds many historically valuable paintings, thrones and coaches which had belonged to the bey.
e9e0d077-22ec-5da6-8968-784248276025.keywords: Architecture; art; painting; stucco; mosaic; marble; ceramics
e9e0d077-22ec-5da6-8968-784248276025.description2: This palace is an excellent example of a typical beylical palace, with an architecture, décor and furnishings that show distinct signs of European, and particularly Italian, influences. The large, tall building is surrounded by trees and orchards. The grand staircase, the marble columns, the marble, ceramic and faience mosaics on the walls, the Italian-style window frames and the Andalusian-style carved stucco all contribute to the decorations' opulent and varied quality, which characterised the 18th and 19th centuries.

ea5004e5-f4e7-5291-8059-9bc54d1ba863.name: Archaeological excavations
ea5004e5-f4e7-5291-8059-9bc54d1ba863.description2: General view of workers behind some scholars who supervise their work. The photograph was taken next to the pyramid of Niuserre at Saqqara in 1904. The photo is printed from glass plate negatives.

eaed42bd-51b3-5083-8735-9c1467c68055.second_name: A colonial postcard for the Italian soldiers fighting in Libya in 1911–12
eaed42bd-51b3-5083-8735-9c1467c68055.description2:
Italian sailors fighting in Libya are portrayed as the heirs of Roman soldiers. On the ground, one can see the personal military equipment of an ancient Roman soldier. The modern sailor holds in his right hand the Roman soldier’s sword and in his left hand an Italian flag.  
Italian colonial rhetoric looked at the Roman Empire as a justification for Italy’s colonial conquests of Libya. The current territory of Libya was for centuries part of the Roman empire.

ebc1fbff-c25e-5ca5-86ba-1be3dbc34cbf.description2: Two of the most important inventions of the 19th century, the rotary and four-colour printing (quadrachrome), are attributed to Augusto Ippolito Marinoni. The new machines changed the printing of journals, achieving up to 18,000 to 20,000 copies per hour. Marinoni had extraordinary success in Paris, where his factory produced 4000 samples of machines which also sold in London, Berlin and Vienna. In Italy at the time, only the journal *Il Secolo* had a "Marinoni".

ecbd97bc-85ed-53b3-ab05-ca13100e4055.description2: Over the centuries the Baths of Diocletian, sacked by the barbarians of Alaric, were abandoned and restored several times. In 1563, Pope Paul IV commissioned Michelangelo to transform it into a church “Santa Maria degli Angeli”. In 1749 the architect Vanvitelli rebuilt it again. For the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored again under the direction of Rodolfo Lanciani for the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, to host the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the "ex provinces". The most incredible reconstruction on display was the Temple of Ancyra (ancient capital of Galatia, in the centre of Minor Asia) dedicated to Augustus and the goddess Roma, based on casts taken by the archaeologist Azeglio Berretti. Included in the display are the famous engraved inscription on bronze tablets, the so-called "Res Gestae” that represents the testament of emperor Augustus.

ece4e33c-7204-5b42-8e58-18b1ae8b4d17.name: *Ruins of Troy: general excavation plan by Mr Schliemann*
ece4e33c-7204-5b42-8e58-18b1ae8b4d17.keywords: Greek antiquities; archaeological excavations; Schliemann; Turkey; plans
ece4e33c-7204-5b42-8e58-18b1ae8b4d17.description2: Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890) was a German businessman who discovered his passion for archaeology whilst travelling. In 1870 he decided to direct an archaeological campaign in Turkey where he discovered the ruins of Troy. Various scandals (stolen objects, scientific errors) quickly destroyed his reputation, and today he is credited only with having created sites which led to important advances in the field. However, this plan of Troy is evidence for Schliemann's efforts to direct the excavations in a rigorous scientific manner.

ed280684-f7be-5238-afc4-1fd992c55380.name: An old exhibition from Tiled Kiosk
ed280684-f7be-5238-afc4-1fd992c55380.description2: The Tiled Kiosk is a pavilion set within the outer walls of Topkapı Palace and dates from 1472. It was built by the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II as a pleasure palace or kiosk. The building was used as the Imperial Museum between 1875 and 1891. In 1953, it was opened to the public as a museum of Turkish and Islamic art, and was later incorporated into the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. The collections of the Tiled Kiosk Museum consist of about 2000 artefacts belonging to the Seljuk and Ottoman eras, dating from the 11th-20th centuries. These artefacts include those that existed when the museum was incorporated into the İstanbul Archaeological Museums due to its closeness and those acquired through excavations, purchases, donations and confiscations.

ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.name: Statue of Athlete – Ephesos
ee1f0807-ca9d-507c-adf4-27f446a10f42.description: After competitions in the *palestra* (sports arena), it was customary for the athletes to clean the sand from their oiled bodies with a strigil, or scraping iron. The Ephesian athlete seen here has already finished this task and – with his hair still soaking in sweat – is cleaning the strigil itself. This statue cannot be attributed to any Greek artist with certainty, yet Roman reproductions in marble and depictions on pottery reliefs and engraved stones speak to a high degree of familiarity with the original.

f0020c49-694c-556a-855c-e631e86ab20b.description2: Field sheet showing a week’s work mapping the environs of Gaza for the Survey of Western Palestine, dated 29th April, 1875. f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.name: *The Great Khan of Damascus*
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.provenance: England; published in Etching depicting *'The Great Khan At Damascus'*, first published in John Carne, *'Syria, The Holy Land, Asia Minor, &c'*, 1836–1838

f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.artist: Painted by William Henry Bartlett; engraved by William H, Kelsall
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.description2: Damascus had long been a major commercial hub in the Middle East, with trading caravans converging on its numerous souqs from all over the Islamic world. Commercial complexes had already flourished in the 18th century and were an integral part of Ottoman modernisation projects in the 19th century. This image gives a wonderful impression of the activities within a traditional Near Eastern khan or market complex in the 19th century. Under high vaulted domes, man and beast are engaged in various activities. Pack animals bring wares or are being unloaded, traders discuss their wares, rest or ponder their accounts. A fountain in the centre provides respite and coolness. On the second floor, figures are visible at the balconies, overlooking the activities below. The print was originally published in Volume I, p. 49, of 'Syria, The Holy Land, Asia Minor &c', printed in 3 series over 2 volumes, drawn by William Henry Bartlett and William Purser, engraved by W. Kelsall, with descriptive text by John Carne. Published by Fisher and Son, with series I and II bound together.

It is important to point out that most of the Spanish collectors and museums not only acquired early Arab pieces of the Middle Ages, but also pieces from the North African or Near Eastern workshops of the mid-19th century or early 20th century, as part of the interest in these countries.

f31fd223-2144-5b45-8b4a-8cf3c4d36bc5.name: *London-Paris-Constantinople* \[…\] *Orient Express. Paris-Munich-Vienna-Budapest-Belgrade & Constantinople: fast and direct service, without your car and without your passport* \[…\] *Winter 1888–89 ...*
f31fd223-2144-5b45-8b4a-8cf3c4d36bc5.description2: Founded in 1872, the Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-lits was originally a Belgian company. Its founder (Georges Nagelmackers) had the idea of creating a luxury train line, without the need for changes at each border, in order to allow wealthier tourists a more comfortable journey. The opening of the famous Orient Express between Paris and Constantinople in 1883 was an extremely successful example of this.

f5b47725-414d-52d8-902a-bee467f7d304.name: *Works for the opening of the Corinth Canal*
f5b47725-414d-52d8-902a-bee467f7d304.author: Maria Dimitriadou
f5b47725-414d-52d8-902a-bee467f7d304.description2:
The Corinth Canal being dug, circa 1885. Photographer unknown.  
The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnesian peninsula from the Greek. The idea of the canal was revived after Greece gained independence but soon abandoned due to economical reasons. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave an new impetus and the following year, the Zaimis government passed a law authorising the construction of the canal, which was formally inaugurated on 23 April 1882. Zaimis assigned the project to the Hungarian István Türr who set up the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe but the company failed and the project was finished by the company of Andeas Syngros. The canal was designed by the Hungarian engineer Béla Gerster with the assistance of the French Vincent Dauzants, a chief engineer of the Suez canal.

f6ce25ef-e196-51ea-878e-f582be55dc3a.name: Petrie and typology
f6ce25ef-e196-51ea-878e-f582be55dc3a.description2: In 1890 Petrie carried out a six-week season of excavations at Tell el-Hesy (as he transliterated it), which he identified, wrongly, as the ancient city of Lachish.  This was the first proper archaeological excavation ever carried out in Palestine, and in the course of this single season Petrie established the principle of dating strata by the pottery which they contained, thus establishing the outlines of the archaeological sequence, which continues to be refined to this day. This section drawing was made by Frederick Jones Bliss, who continued Petrie’s excavations from 1892–1894.

f6f098bc-4e9c-5171-b766-ca9c47aabe50.name: New maps
f6f098bc-4e9c-5171-b766-ca9c47aabe50.description2: Sgt. George Armstrong, R.E., who was a key member of the Survey Party, later made a 3D ‘Raised Contour Map’ of Palestine from the 2D maps originally produced. This was shown all over the western world, and won him a medal at the St. Louis World’s Fair in 1903. It was the first such map ever constructed of Palestine, and served to introduce scholars and the public to the nature of the landscape in a way that no previous maps had done.

f92e54e2-12d0-5aaf-9ae2-ccb42b9f2df7.description2: Robertson’s Istanbul photographs are concerned primarily with the city’s historical monuments. They reveal the city’s magnificent Byzantine and Ottoman structures from different angles and with close-ups taken in an approach that is usually quite aesthetic. A frequently employed device in Robertson's photographs is the inclusion of the one or more human figures in the foreground – indeed, this is something of a trademark of Robertson’s work. In this photo, the monuments in the Hippodrome are surrounded by protective fences.

f9783fd3-09a2-5548-be22-593259d96e06.name: Fragment of the Parthenon frieze
f9783fd3-09a2-5548-be22-593259d96e06.description: The climax of the Greater Panathenaia, the chief festival of Athens, held in honour of Athena, was a procession which ended with the presentation of the newly woven peplos (a woman’s garment) to the tutelary goddess of the city. This is the subject of the frieze around the cella of the Parthenon, the temple on the Athenian Acropolis. This fragment shows two bearded elder citizens of Athens in conversation.

fa8521f5-5b5a-5099-8913-7567fa1ba0ab.name: A moneylender's kit
fa8521f5-5b5a-5099-8913-7567fa1ba0ab.description2: In the first half of the 19th century, before the first banks were founded in Wallachia and Moldavia, moneylenders were the ones who dealt with money loaning and with currency exchange, in an economy which did not have yet a national coin. In Romanian they used to be called "zarafi", a term borrowed from the Turkish language. Most of them were Greek, Armenian and Jewish. They often travelled abroad to buy money, one of their main destinations being Istanbul.

fb2abd3f-4014-5c92-a525-a24db70c968b.name: Map of the 1877–1878 war
fb2abd3f-4014-5c92-a525-a24db70c968b.description2: This map shows the theatre of operations during the Russian-Ottoman war of 1877–1878, which for Romania represents her independence war. In April 1877, Romania signed a secret military convention with Russia, who was on the eve of a new war with the Ottoman Empire, allowing her troops to cross the Romanian territory in order to get south of the Danube. Because in May the Ottomans bombed some Romanian ports on the Danube without a previous war declaration, the Parliament proclaimed Romania’s independence and decided the country’s entrance in the war. By the beginning of 1878, the Russo-Romanian army was victorious. At the peace Congress of Berlin (June-July 1878) Romania’s independence was recognized, but she had to cede Russia the south of Bessarabia in exchange for a part of Dobruja.

fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.name: Palais-Musée du Bardo
fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.history: The museum occupies just a part of the entire Palais du Bardo, a collection of buildings constructed from the early 15th century onwards. It was built in the style of Andalusian princely residences, but also shows traces of North African Tunisian and Italian architectural influences dating to the Husainid period when it underwent a series of modifications. The museum was opened and received its first archaeological collections on 7 May 1888 by the Bey of Tunisia and the French Resident-General. It remains, to this day, one of the most important archaeological museums in the world, and is particularly renowned for its excellent collection of Roman mosaics.

fe6cec92-b619-55f4-a18b-3a0f8fd470af.description2: The Musée du Bardo receives more than 500,000 visitors each year. It is divided into three floors, each holding thousands of exceptionally valuable items, all of which tell the story of a country at the crossroads of multiple civilisations. Visitors can admire mosaics on the floors and walls, the statues, funerary steles, ceramics, jewellery, works of art and bronze and marble sculptures, ranging from the prehistoric era to Punic, Roman and Byzantine times.

ff78af46-329b-5d7b-810a-cacb6d484374.name: Umm al-Rasas
ff78af46-329b-5d7b-810a-cacb6d484374.dates: Roman-Present; identified in 1896 by J. Germer-Durand
ff78af46-329b-5d7b-810a-cacb6d484374.author: Mohammad Najjar
ff78af46-329b-5d7b-810a-cacb6d484374.history: The World Heritage Site of Umm al-Rasas (Kastron Mefa'a, Kastrom Mefa'a) is an archaeological site in Jordan which contains ruins from the Roman, Byzantine, and early Muslim periods. The most important monument in the site was the mosaic floor of the Church of St Stephen. This biggest mosaic floor in Jordan – which was built in 785 AD – depicts the most important cities in Jordan, Palestine and Egypt. The fact that the mosaic floor was constructed during the Abbasid period reflects the spirit of tolerance and co-existence of the Muslim and Christian communities during that period. Umm al-Rasas was visited by H.B. Tristram in 1872 and subsequently identified in 1896 by J. Germer-Durand with the Biblical and Late Antiquity city of Mephaath.
ff78af46-329b-5d7b-810a-cacb6d484374.keywords: World Heritage Site; frontier station; Archaeological investigations; churches; mosaic panels; Tristram
ff78af46-329b-5d7b-810a-cacb6d484374.description2: The town of Umm al-Rasas was enclosed in an almost square (app.160x155 meters) enclosure surrounded by fortification walls and 24 towers. The main gateway was from the east. Two small gates were positioned at the north and the south sides. These were blocked later. Archaeological investigations at the site were concentrated on the four churches identified inside the fortification walls, including the church of the Rivers and the church of the Palm tree. These were named after the main component of the mosaic panels on the floors. At least 11 other churches were identified outside the enclosure to the north. The most prominent of them are the church of St. Stephen with its famous mosaic panels of 15 major towns of Jordan and Palestine of the time.
